title: Claude Fable, Claude Tag, and Anthropic's Culture — Cat Wu & Thariq Shihipar ft Simon Willison
talk_summary: Anthropic's Cat Wu and Thariq Shihipar describe how Claude Code/Claude Tag are used internally: proactive channel-resident agents landing 65% of product PRs, a months-long trust ramp to remove humans from code review, and eval-driven prompt/tool simplification. They also detail auto-mode permission classification, credential-injection proxying, and per-model system prompts.

takeaways.technique: Graduated trust ramp for LLM review, gated by file area
takeaways.what_they_do: Start with human review on everything; only after LLM review demonstrably catches 100% of issues in a file set do they drop the human for those files, keeping code owners on core files.
takeaways.evidence_quote: for code changes that touch these files code review is catching a 100% of the issues there. So we actually don't need a human
takeaways.numbers: 6+ month process; 100% issue catch rate per file area before removing human

takeaways.what_they_do: When an incident occurs, they inspect the PR that caused it, update the reviewer to catch that class, and add the PR to an eval set so future reviewer changes can't regress it.
takeaways.evidence_quote: we look at the PRs that cause the incident and we say okay how do we update code review to catch that and then we also take those PRs and add it to an eval set

takeaways.what_they_do: They keep different system prompts per model; the 80% token reduction only applies to frontier models, older/cheaper models keep the full verbose prompt.
takeaways.numbers: 80% system-prompt token reduction on frontier models

takeaways.technique: Remove over-constraints and 'always' rules; prefer context over prohibitions
takeaways.what_they_do: They audited prompts for instructions that are only ~90% true, softened 'always verify' into contextual guidance, and cut examples and hard 'do not' rules that conflict with user instructions.
takeaways.evidence_quote: we found a few cases where yes, this statement is like 90% true, but there's like a real 10% of cases where this is not true

takeaways.what_they_do: A proxy inserts real credentials on the fly when the agent calls an allowlisted host, so the agent can use the API but cannot read the token.
takeaways.evidence_quote: we insert it on the fly when the agent tries to make a data dog request

takeaways.technique: Proactive channel-resident agent with shared team memory
takeaways.what_they_do: A persistent agent in a channel monitors events (bug reports), opens PRs, tags the right owner, and stores team preferences as a markdown file per channel that all instances read/write.
takeaways.evidence_quote: monitor every bug report in this channel, put up a PR to fix it, and tag the engineer who last touched this part of the codebase
takeaways.numbers: 65% of product PRs landed by internal Claude Tag
